```{python}
import _maps

from IPython.display import HTML, Markdown, display
from itables import init_notebook_mode
from itables import show as ishow

# `connected=False` embeds DataTables rather than fetching it from a CDN, so
# the published page has no external dependency and works offline. It costs
# about 200 kB, and only this page uses it.
init_notebook_mode(all_interactive=False, connected=False)


def table(df, page=25, order=None):
    """A sortable, searchable ranking table.

    Not `display(df)`: pandas caps its HTML repr at 60 rows, which silently
    truncated the 352-row all-aerodromes ranking to the first 60 -- a ranking that
    stops two thirds of the way down, with nothing on the page saying so.
    """
    # `allow_html=True` is required for the ICAO column: without it itables
    # escapes the anchor tags and the reader sees the raw `<a href=...>` markup
    # as text in the cell, with nothing clickable.
    ishow(df, maxBytes=0, lengthMenu=[25, 50, 100, 500],
          pageLength=page, scrollX=True, allow_html=True,
          order=order if order is not None else [],
          classes="display compact")

def downloads(which, period):
    """The download buttons for one ranking table.

    Plain anchors with Bootstrap's button classes, not a DataTables export
    plugin: `init_notebook_mode(connected=False)` above embeds DataTables so the
    page has no external dependency, and itables 2.9 does not ship the Buttons
    extension in that bundle -- asking for `buttons=[...]` silently produces a
    table with no buttons on it. Serving files the build already wrote needs no
    JavaScript at all and works with it disabled.
    """
    stem = download_stem(which, period)
    return Markdown(
        f'<a class="btn btn-outline-primary btn-sm" role="button" '
        f'href="downloads/{stem}.xlsx" download>Download Excel</a>&nbsp;'
        f'<a class="btn btn-outline-secondary btn-sm" role="button" '
        f'href="downloads/{stem}.csv" download>Download CSV</a>'
        f'\n\n<small>Every row and column of the table below, for '
        f'**{period}**. Blank cells are blank rather than dashed, so a '
        f'spreadsheet reads the column as numbers.</small>'
    )


HAVE = bool(_data.periods_available())
LATEST = _data.latest() if HAVE else None
```

## The fleet

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAVE:
    a = _data.load_ranking("a", LATEST)
    b = _data.load_ranking("b", LATEST)

    def _summary(s, label, pct=False):
        s = pd.Series(s).dropna()
        if s.empty:
            return {"metric": label, "n": 0}
        f = (lambda v: f"{v:.1f}%") if pct else (lambda v: f"{v:.3f}")
        return {
            "metric": label, "n": len(s),
            "median": f(s.median()),
            "IQR": f"{f(s.quantile(.25))} – {f(s.quantile(.75))}",
            "p10": f(s.quantile(.10)), "p90": f(s.quantile(.90)),
        }

    display(Markdown(
        "Where the aerodromes sit as a group, before looking at any one of "
        "them. Each row is one measure; the columns are its spread across "
        "aerodromes — the middle value, the middle half, and the worst and "
        "best tenths. The first three rows are the point of this site: half "
        "the measured aerodromes receive less than a fifth of a typical "
        "taxi-out. The two “seen” rows below them are near 100% for most "
        "aerodromes — the worst tenth reaches down to 87%, which is the only "
        "place this measure separates anything, and is why it cannot be the "
        "headline."
    ))
    display(Markdown(explain_block(
        ["dep_signal_p50", "arr_signal_p50", "coverage_index", "detection_pct"],
        title="What these measures are",
    )))
    # Plain labels, and the same measures the tables below use. This showed
    # bin occupancy under the word "observed" and a reach row that appears
    # nowhere else on the site -- both left over from earlier versions.
    rows = [
        _summary(a.dep_signal_p50, "Taxi-out received — measured aerodromes"),
        _summary(a.arr_signal_p50, "Taxi-in received — measured aerodromes"),
        _summary(a.coverage_index, "Coverage index — measured aerodromes"),
        _summary(b.detection_pct, "Flights seen — all aerodromes", pct=True),
        _summary(a.detection_pct, "Flights seen — aerodromes with measured "
                                  "times", pct=True),
    ]
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

```{python}
        f"- **taxi-in received** — the same for arrivals, over the taxi-in.\n\n"
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAVE:
    # Same builder as the download, for the same reason as above.
    t = all_aerodromes_table(b)
    display(Markdown(explain_block(ALL_COLS)))
    display(downloads("all-aerodromes", LATEST))
    t = t.copy()
    # Fixed-width strings, not floats, and only on the display path. itables
    # renders a missing float as the literal "NaN", and 90 of these 352 rows
    # are missing -- 89 because the aerodrome is measured and its real figure
    # is in the table above, one because it cannot be computed. They cluster at
    # the top, so the first thing a reader saw was five rows of "NaN".
    #
    # Zero-padded to three decimals so DataTables' lexicographic sort over the
    # resulting strings orders them exactly as a numeric sort would; the em
    # dash sorts to one end, which is what a blank should do. The exported file
    # keeps the real NaN, because an em dash in a spreadsheet makes the whole
    # column text.
    t["dep_signal_est"] = (t["dep_signal_est"].map(lambda v: f"{v:.3f}")
                           .where(t["dep_signal_est"].notna())
                           .fillna("—"))
    t["icao"] = [f'<a href="airports/{i}.html">{i}</a>' for i in t["icao"]]
    table(rename(t))
```

## What "coverage" means here

Two different questions, and the difference between them is the point.

**How much of its time on the ground was received?** This is the one the site
is built on. The taxi is bounded by real stand and runway times, the feed
should deliver a report every 5 seconds, and we count how many of those
expected reports actually arrived. Answerable only where those times are
recorded — and the answer varies enormously.

**Was the flight seen at all?** One position report anywhere between take-off
and landing is enough. It is reported because it is answerable everywhere and
because it sets a floor — an aerodrome scoring low here is invisible to the
network rather than merely poorly tracked — but almost everywhere in Europe the
answer is "yes, above 99% of the time", so on its own it distinguishes almost
nothing.

The coverage index multiplies the two. An aerodrome can score 99% on the second
and near zero on the first, and several do: the aircraft is tracked in the air
and invisible on the ground.

Between those two questions sits a third. Network Manager predicts a taxi
duration for every European departure, and that prediction is unbiased even
though it is loose — so for an aerodrome with no measured times, the *median*
share of its taxi-out that arrived can still be estimated. That figure is the
last column of the second table. Nothing equivalent exists for arrivals: no
in-block time is recorded outside APDF, so there is no window to measure a
taxi-in against, and the index — which needs both — stays a measured-aerodrome number.

## What the ranking does not say

- An aerodrome outside the ingested area is **absent**, not ranked last — see
  the map above. Its movements were never sampled, so any figure for it would
  measure the boundary rather than the receiver network. Flights *to* those
  aerodromes still count at their European end.
- **A low coverage index has two possible causes, and they need different
  fixes.** Position reports arrive as one continuous stream per aircraft, with
  nothing in them marking where one flight ends and the next begins, so the
  flights have to be cut out of that stream first. When the cut goes wrong,
  coverage looks worse than the receivers deserve:

  - *split* — one flight cut into several tracks. Coverage is measured against
    the largest piece, so the rest is not counted: within the same aerodrome a
    split departure's track starts a median 392 seconds later than a clean one.
    This aerodrome's coverage is understated by roughly that much.
  - *merged* — two flights left in one track. The worse failure, but a
    different one: only one flight comes out, so the other is absent from the
    output entirely. The survivor's own coverage shows no consistent shift, and
    merged movements are 0.8% of the sample.

  The **tracking errors** column adds the two together, as a share of that
  aerodrome's movements. A high figure means its coverage is probably
  understated and some of its movements are missing — neither of which is a
  reception problem. Each aerodrome's page breaks it into split and merged
  separately, which is the distinction that matters when diagnosing one.
- The two tiers are not comparable and are never merged into one table.
